hints: Think about what a chloroplast looks like inside. It is an organelle inside a eukaryotic cell, but it has its own tiny genome and its own ribosomes to make some of its own proteins.
Recall the two big differences examiners love: 70S (small, prokaryotic) versus 80S (large, eukaryotic cytosol) ribosomes, and circular, naked DNA versus linear DNA with histones.
walkthrough:
**Recall a typical prokaryotic cell**

A typical bacterium has no nucleus. Its DNA is a single circular molecule free in the cytoplasm, and its ribosomes for protein synthesis are all the small 70S type.

**Recall the structure of a chloroplast**

A chloroplast also has its own small circular DNA loop (not linear chromosomes) and its own small 70S ribosomes in the stroma. This is strong evidence for endosymbiosis, that chloroplasts evolved from engulfed prokaryotes.

**Put them together**

Both structures share BOTH features: 70S ribosomes AND circular DNA. So we need the option that includes both, not only one of them.

options.A: Correct. Both chloroplasts and prokaryotic cells contain 70S ribosomes and circular, naked DNA.
options.B: Incomplete. Both do have 70S ribosomes, but they also both have circular DNA, so saying only is wrong.
options.C: Wrong ribosome. 80S ribosomes are found in the eukaryotic cytosol, not in prokaryotes or chloroplasts which have 70S.
options.D: Incomplete. Both do have circular DNA, but they also both have 70S ribosomes, so saying only is wrong.
